Which iPad should you buy? With four different models, optional 5G cellular connectivity, multiple storage capacities, colors, and even refurbished options to consider, choosing the right iPad isn’t always straightforward.

Apple’s newest iPad is the iPad mini (A20 Pro), which went on sale November 6 with an 8.5-inch OLED display and a thinner, lighter design. The M4 iPad Air arrived in March 2026, and the M5 iPad Pro launched in October 2025. The standard iPad still uses the A16 chip from March 2025 and is the only iPad in Apple’s lineup without Apple Intelligence. Reports point to a replacement in the first half of 2027 that could add Apple Intelligence support.

This in-depth buying guide compares every iPad Apple currently sells and explains which model is best for different types of users. We’ll help you decide which offers the best value, how much storage you really need, which screen size is right for you, and whether it’s worth paying extra for a cellular model. We also look at whether new models are expected soon, so you can decide if now is the right time to buy. After our recommendations, you’ll find more detailed advice on displays, storage, processors, accessories, and Wi-Fi versus cellular.

The bad news is that Apple raised prices across the iPad range in June 2026, citing an unprecedented rise in component costs. In a statement, the company said it had “never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly” and explained that, while it had absorbed the extra costs for as long as possible, it had “reached a point where we need to begin raising prices on a number of products.” As a result, some iPads now cost hundreds of dollars more. We’ve updated all prices throughout this guide.

With prices in mind, if you are looking for a bargain, be sure to take a look at our roundup of the Best iPad Deals this Black Friday.

Best iPad to buy in 2026

If you mainly want an iPad for browsing, streaming, video calls, or the kids, the standard iPad (A16) is our budget pick. It starts at $449/£429 and has enough power for everyday apps and games.

If you want the smallest iPad, choose the iPad mini (A20 Pro). Its compact design is ideal for reading one-handed or playing games on the go. At $699/£699, it costs only $50/£50 less than the 11-inch iPad Air, so choose the Air if you’d get more use out of a bigger screen

How much storage do iPads need?

iPads in the current lineup offer anywhere from 128GB to 2TB of storage, but if you are looking at an old, refurbished, or preowned iPad you could be confronted with 64GB or even 32GB storage, which isn’t enough. But what storage capacity do you really need for an iPad?

Well, first of all, remember that you can’t upgrade the storage of an iPad at a later date: this is your limit from now until you buy another iPad, so aim high and buy as much storage as you can afford. It’s better to spend an extra few pounds now than to buy an entire new iPad in six months.

Storage capacity is mainly used up by three things: music, photos, and videos. If you want to keep lots of films or TV shows–or even a few, to be honest–then you need high storage: probably 256GB or higher for video fans. If you’re buying an iPad with the kids in mind, remember that you’ll want storage space for multiple episodes of their favorite show on a long car journey.

The same applies if you have large photo or music libraries, although iCloud Photos and iTunes Match make it possible to keep your stuff in the cloud and access it remotely. The problem with iCloud Photos is that it will store low-res versions of all your images, from all your devices, on your iPad. If your library is huge then even these low-res versions of images can take up a lot of space on your iPad. If you don’t have a lot of storage on your iPad then avoid using iCloud Photos.

The other thing that will fill up your storage is apps, especially games which will use up a lot of space. For that reason gamers should aim high on storage: The iPad, iPad Air and iPad mini start with 128GB and the Pro begins at 256GB. We recommend getting what you can afford. Our best advice is to only consider the current or previous generation iPads when looking at refurbished models, then you are less likely to be caught out by a sub-par tablet.

Buying a refurbished iPad from a reputable company is definitely preferable to buying a used iPad from someone on eBay. It’s too often the case that secondhand iPads sold that way end up as useless bricks because the person selling it didn’t properly log out of their account.

Another way to save money is to buy from a reseller who is selling discontinued stock at a discount. We often see resellers significantly dropping the price on older iPad models that are usually just one generation out of date—just beware, they sell out quick!

Should you buy the newest iPad generation?

Speaking of older iPads, even if functioning perfectly right now, older models will reach the end of their useful life sooner than the newest models and that is a good reason to avoid buying an iPad that is more than one or two generations old. But keep in mind that iPads tend to start slowing down at around two to three years of age; at the four- or five-year mark you should expect noticeable loss of performance and you won’t be able to get all the latest software updates. The current iPad range launched in 2024 and 2026, the most recent being the iPad Air in March 2026 and the oldest being the iPad mini in October 2024.

Another reason to buy a recent iPad is the operating system it runs. Apple only supports recent versions of iPadOS with security updates, so that could mean that only iPadOS 26 and iPad OS 18 get security updates, although Apple has been known to update older iPadOS versions when necessary. So, while you don’t have to buy the newest generation, we would recommend that you buy one that was launched relatively recently to be sure that Apple will support it for as long as you intend to own it. How much storage do iPads need?

iPads in the current lineup offer anywhere from 128GB to 2TB of storage, but if you are looking at an old, refurbished, or preowned iPad you could be confronted with 64GB or even 32GB storage, which isn’t enough. But what storage capacity do you really need for an iPad?

Well, first of all, remember that you can’t upgrade the storage of an iPad at a later date: this is your limit from now until you buy another iPad, so aim high and buy as much storage as you can afford. It’s better to spend an extra few pounds now than to buy an entire new iPad in six months.

Storage capacity is mainly used up by three things: music, photos, and videos. If you want to keep lots of films or TV shows–or even a few, to be honest–then you need high storage: probably 256GB or higher for video fans. If you’re buying an iPad with the kids in mind, remember that you’ll want storage space for multiple episodes of their favorite show on a long car journey.

The same applies if you have large photo or music libraries, although iCloud Photos and iTunes Match make it possible to keep your stuff in the cloud and access it remotely. The problem with iCloud Photos is that it will store low-res versions of all your images, from all your devices, on your iPad. If your library is huge then even these low-res versions of images can take up a lot of space on your iPad. If you don’t have a lot of storage on your iPad then avoid using iCloud Photos.

The other thing that will fill up your storage is apps, especially games which will use up a lot of space. For that reason gamers should aim high on storage: The iPad, iPad Air and iPad mini start with 128GB and the Pro begins at 256GB. We recommend getting what you can afford. Our best advice is to only consider the current or previous generation iPads when looking at refurbished models, then you are less likely to be caught out by a sub-par tablet.

Buying a refurbished iPad from a reputable company is definitely preferable to buying a used iPad from someone on eBay. It’s too often the case that secondhand iPads sold that way end up as useless bricks because the person selling it didn’t properly log out of their account.

Another way to save money is to buy from a reseller who is selling discontinued stock at a discount. We often see resellers significantly dropping the price on older iPad models that are usually just one generation out of date—just beware, they sell out quick!

Should you buy the newest iPad generation?

Speaking of older iPads, even if functioning perfectly right now, older models will reach the end of their useful life sooner than the newest models and that is a good reason to avoid buying an iPad that is more than one or two generations old. But keep in mind that iPads tend to start slowing down at around two to three years of age; at the four- or five-year mark you should expect noticeable loss of performance and you won’t be able to get all the latest software updates. The current iPad range launched in 2024 and 2026, the most recent being the iPad Air in March 2026 and the oldest being the iPad mini in October 2024.

Another reason to buy a recent iPad is the operating system it runs. Apple only supports recent versions of iPadOS with security updates, so that could mean that only iPadOS 26 and iPad OS 18 get security updates, although Apple has been known to update older iPadOS versions when necessary. So, while you don’t have to buy the newest generation, we would recommend that you buy one that was launched relatively recently to be sure that Apple will support it for as long as you intend to own it. A new job listing for a Senior Engineering Manager at Apple’s Cupertino campus has given away an open secret: Apple is working on an autonomous, proactive AI agent. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”

AI agents that operate continuously and proactively in the background are the latest hot item, and some think are the next big frontier in consumer AI. It’s the natural successor to chatbots, and is often perceived as the big step that will get the whole world hooked on AI.

Currently, AI agents are extremely popular in the App Store. Meta’s Muse is the #2 free app, behind only TikTok. Chatbots that have added agentic capabilities hold other top spots: ChatGPT is #3, Claude is #5, and Gemini is #7.

Each of these has varying degrees of autonomy, and many of the Mac apps from these companies can access your Mac’s data and operate its app. Google’s Gemini Mac app was just updated to be able to use your Mac for you, for example.

Apple’s job posting makes it clear that the company is building its own similar product. The job description is as follows:

People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service. We’re building AI agents that can do the same. We’re a team of engineers, AI applied researchers, and systems specialists working on general-purpose computer-use agents. These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.

As a senior leader in this org, you will own the technical direction and delivery of our agent platform and the AI capabilities built on it. You will lead and develop a team of managers and engineers. You will also build the AI and systems talent that will define what we can ship next. You’ll work closely with partner teams across Siri, UI frameworks, and AFM and more. Your job is to turn their capabilities, and ours, into agents that are capable, reliable, and safe.

The posted job listing is for a senior management position, someone who will, “Set the technical vision, roadmap, and quality bar for AI agents that work across apps, browsers, terminals, code, and APIs.” If that is the case, and Apple is trying to assemble its team and direct the vision for the project now, then it is at least a year behind its competitors. Competing services have proactive and autonomous AI agents available to consumers today–even if Apple races ahead at top speed, it’s hard to imagine a similar product reaching users until at least the fall of 2027, by which time Meta, OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic will be on their second or third generation of consumer AI agents.

Like most things, except the average human being, devices are forever getting slimmer and lighter. Apple’s iPhone Air took thinness to a new level, with the phone measuring only 0.22 inches (5.64mm) at the waist.

Putting the Air in a case seems perverse, but clamping a power bank on its skinny body is sometimes going to be a necessity—especially given that its own internal battery is smaller than other iPhones (3,149mAh vs 3,692mAh for the iPhone 17 released at the same time) in order to make it so damn flat.

Power banks have been getting into the slimming act too. Recently the BMX SolidSafe Air 5K and Baseus Picogo Air AM71 Magnetic Power Bank drew in a dead-skinny heat at a depth of just 0.27 inches (6.8mm).

Momax

Just how thin is the Momax 1-Power S.Pass Air power bank?

At just 6.3mm thick, the Momax 1-Power S.Pass Air takes the crown as the thinnest magnetic power bank we’ve tested. Momax lists it at 6.0mm, with a tolerance of ±0.2mm, and our digital caliper put our sample at 6.3mm. That extra 0.3mm is an extremely slender margin that few will notice.

Looking at it, it’s difficult to imagine a power bank getting any thinner due to the USB-C port nearly touching the edges. But Apple managed to get the Air down to 0.22 inches (5.64mm) so it must be possible. The only other thing holding back skinnier power banks is the battery inside, and any included safety and cooling techs.

While it carries the label ‘5K’ for 5000mAh (milliamp hours), a more accurate measure is in watt hours, and the Momax battery itself is rated at 19.25Wh—over the average 19Wh for a 5K portable charger.

Simon Jary

How does the Momax 1-Power S.Pass Air power bank perform?

We test every portable charger in the same way: run an iPhone down to 0% and then connect the power bank. We do it up to three times and publish the best result. A 5K power bank will run dry itself before the iPhone has reached 100%—the average Macworld Recharge Score is 76%, with the highest we’ve tested reaching 90% (Ugreen MagFlow Air).

The Momax 1-Power S.Pass Air scored 73%, a little below average. While not at the top of the recharge scores, it promises to take your depleted iPhone back to nearly three-quarters of power while staying super slim in your pocket or handbag.

Its slimness might explain the lower recharge score as power banks lose efficiency when hot, and possible the slim profile increases this and other wireless factors.

It’s a Qi2 wireless charger, so maxes at 15W power output. Look to a 10K power bank for 25W and up to 200% recharge scores, but of course you’ll not get anything as slim as the S.Pass Air 5K.

You’ll get a faster charge if you use the power bank’s USB-C port with a cable to connect your iPhone, as that outputs at up to 22.5W.

Momax also sells a larger model, the 1-Power S.Pass 10000mAh Semi-Solid-State Magnetic Battery Pack. This has advantages such as 25W wireless charging (30W wired) and a larger battery capacity (38.8Wh) as well as utilizing the more durable semi-solid-state battery technology. On the downside, it’s over twice as deep as the 5K, at 0.57 inches (14.5mm) and 208g in weight. Turn it on its side and you’ll barely notice it, but it looks gorgeous front on, although I do worry it might attract scratches if left tumbling around in a bag or frequently drawn from a rough trouser pocket.

It’s available in Dusky Cherry – perfect for the latest Burgundy iPhone 18 Pro – as well as Silver and Titanium.

If you want the leanest power bank available today, the Momax 1-Power S.Pass Air is the real skinny. It looks great, will get lost in a pocket, and takes your iPhone to nearly 75% from 0% when you need it most.

More frequent heart-rate and HRV tracking

Both watches have redesigned optical and electrical heart sensors, including larger, more power-efficient green LEDs. Background heart-rate readings are taken every five seconds, while heart rate variability (HRV) can be measured as often as every five minutes. These more frequent measurements provide a fuller picture of your activity and recovery throughout the day.

The improvement is particularly significant for background monitoring. In Macwelt’s testing, Apple Watch Series 11 already recorded heart rate every five seconds during a workout, but its overnight readings were much less frequent and irregular. Across one sample night, the average interval was 4 minutes 39 seconds. Series 12’s five-second background readings therefore provide a denser record between workouts.

HRV measures variation in the time between heartbeats. The watches distinguish between Recovery HRV, which helps assess shorter-term stress and recovery, and overall HRV, which provides insight into longer-term health trends. Recovery HRV is also included in overnight Vitals, where it is compared with your personal baseline. A new daytime Vitals view shows heart rate and HRV, helping you spot changes outside your usual ranges.

Readiness: Should you push harder or take it easy?

Readiness combines recent activity, training load, daytime and overnight vitals, and sleep data into a score from 0 to 10. It provides one of four recommendations:

  • Recover: 0–1
  • Pace Yourself: 2–4
  • Ready: 5–7
  • Go For It: 8–10

The score updates throughout the day as you exercise, rest or take a nap. Open the Readiness app to see how activity, vitals and sleep are influencing it.

You’ll need to set up Activity, Sleep and overnight Vitals, enter your health details, and wear the watch to bed for at least seven nights before receiving a score. Readiness is a wellness guide: it doesn’t account for every medical condition or medication and shouldn’t be your sole basis for deciding whether it is safe to exercise.

Returning health features

Both watches retain ECG, high and low heart-rate notifications, irregular-rhythm notifications, blood oxygen tracking, sleep stages, sleep score, sleep apnea notifications and temperature-based Cycle Tracking. These features are also available on earlier compatible Apple Watches, although availability varies by model and region.

Hypertension notifications look for patterns associated with chronic high blood pressure over 30-day periods; they don’t provide a blood-pressure reading. The feature also supports earlier compatible models, and availability on Series 12 and Ultra 4 remains subject to regulatory clearance in some regions.

Do the new sensors affect battery life?

In Macwelt’s comparison of the Series 12 and Series 11, Halyna Kubiv recorded more background activity on the newer watch but lower energy consumption during the period after a hike.

That comparison covered a single day, and the watches differed in iPhone pairing and display use. It suggests the additional monitoring can be efficient, but doesn’t prove it has no effect on battery life.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 processor: What processor do they use?

Both watches use Apple’s new S11 chip, replacing the S10 used by Series 11 and Ultra 3.

Apple’s specifications list:

  • 64-bit dual-core processor
  • 4-core Neural Engine
  • 64GB storage
  • Secure hardware for Audio Intelligence processing

The S10 also had a 64-bit dual-core CPU, four-core Neural Engine and 64GB of storage, so the headline specifications alone don’t reveal how much faster S11 actually is. Apple calls it its “most powerful wearable chip”, but notably hasn’t provided a percentage CPU or GPU performance improvement over S10, and its technical specifications don’t list a separate GPU core count.

That means the more important S11 improvements appear to be what the chip enables rather than raw benchmark performance.

It works with the new Health Sensing System, supports Siri AI and powers the new Audio Intelligence functionality. Apple has also emphasised efficiency, particularly in relation to higher-frequency sensor readings and Ultra 4’s improved battery life.

The new Audio Intelligence system includes a Secure Exclave, a hardware-isolated area of the S11 that processes audio separately and deletes raw audio immediately after processing.
